questions.title: Does a securities‑fraud indictment require a traditional property interest, or can “money or property” be satisfied by inducing a purchase?
questions.question_body: In United States v. Constantinescu the Fifth Circuit reversed a dismissal, saying the indictment alleged a scheme to defraud followers of “money or property” by fraudulently inducing them to buy securities. How does the court interpret the phrase “money or property” under 18 U.S.C. § 1348? Is the induced purchase of a security sufficient to satisfy the property‑interest element, even though the victim ultimately receives a market‑value security?

questions.title: What is the difference between the “right‑to‑control” theory and the “fraudulent‑inducement” theory in federal fraud statutes?
questions.question_body: The opinion contrasts Ciminelli’s rejected right‑to‑control theory with the Supreme Court’s acceptance of the fraudulent‑inducement theory in Kousisis. Could someone explain the doctrinal distinction between these two theories and why one is permissible for a securities‑fraud charge while the other is not?

questions.title: Is actual economic loss required to prove the “intent to defraud” element under 18 U.S.C. § 1348?
questions.question_body: Defendants in Constantinescu argue the indictment fails to allege intent to harm because they only sought profit. The Fifth Circuit cites Kousisis, which says victim loss isn’t required. How does “intent to defraud” get satisfied if the victim does not suffer a net pecuniary loss? Does the government need any evidence of the victim’s harm at all?

questions.title: What standard of review does the Fifth Circuit apply to a motion to dismiss for insufficiency of an indictment?
questions.question_body: The opinion states the court reviews the sufficiency of an indictment de novo, citing United States v. Rafoi. How does that de novo standard differ from a more deferential review (e.g., for facial sufficiency), and what specific elements must the court look for when evaluating a fraud‐related indictment?

questions.title: How does the Fifth Circuit treat the securities‑fraud statute’s “scheme to defraud” element when the alleged scheme is a pump‑and‑dump via social‑media posts?
questions.question_body: The opinion says a “scheme to defraud” requires a material misrepresentation intended to obtain money or property. In a pump‑and‑dump where the defendants post false statements on social media, what constitutes the “scheme” for purposes of § 1348? Does each false post count as a separate act, or is the overall campaign treated as one scheme?

questions.title: Can a defendant be charged with conspiracy to commit securities fraud under § 1349 if the underlying fraud theory is the fraudulent‑inducement theory?
questions.question_body: The indictment includes conspiracy to commit securities fraud (18 U.S.C. § 1349) alongside substantive fraud counts. Does the Supreme Court’s approval of the fraudulent‑inducement theory automatically extend to the conspiracy charge, or must the indictment separately allege agreement to pursue that specific theory?

questions.title: What is the “double jeopardy” purpose of an indictment, and how does the Fifth Circuit ensure it is met in fraud cases?
questions.question_body: The opinion cites United States v. Gaytan, noting an indictment must provide a “double jeopardy defense against future prosecutions.” In the context of securities‑fraud prosecutions, how does the court verify that the indictment’s allegations are sufficiently particular to protect the defendants from later re‑prosecution on the same conduct?

questions.title: Why did the Fifth Circuit rely on mail‑ and wire‑fraud precedent to interpret the securities‑fraud statute in Constantinescu?
questions.question_body: The opinion mentions that § 1348 “borrows key concepts from the mail and wire fraud statutes” and that the court often relies on those cases. What are the key parallels, and are there any limits to using mail‑/wire‑fraud jurisprudence to resolve securities‑fraud elements?
